content: Isaac Newton, also known as Sir Isaac Newton, was an English physicist, mathematician, astronomer, natural philosopher, alchemist, and theologian. His groundbreaking work, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in 1687, is widely regarded as one of the most influential books in the history of science. In this work, Newton formulated the laws of universal gravitation and the three laws of motion, which became the foundation of classical mechanics. These principles dominated the scientific understanding of the physical universe for over three centuries and remain fundamental to modern engineering. Newton demonstrated that the same natural laws govern the motion of objects on Earth and celestial bodies. By showing the consistency between Kepler's laws of planetary motion and his own theory of gravitation, he eliminated lingering doubts about heliocentrism and significantly advanced the scientific revolution. In mechanics, he introduced the principles of conservation of momentum and angular momentum. In optics, he invented the reflecting telescope and developed a theory of color based on his observation that a prism decomposes white light into a visible spectrum. He also formulated an empirical law of cooling and studied the speed of sound. In mathematics, Newton shares credit with Gottfried Leibniz for the development of differential and integral calculus. He also generalized the binomial theorem, devised Newton's method for approximating the roots of a function, and contributed to the study of power series. Newton was deeply religious, though his beliefs were unorthodox. He wrote extensively on Biblical hermeneutics, producing more work on theology than on natural science. In a 2005 poll conducted by the Royal Society, Newton was deemed more influential to the history of science than Albert Einstein. Newton was born on January 4, 1643, at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, England. His birth was recorded as December 25, 1642, under the Julian calendar, which England still used at the time. Born prematurely, he was a small and frail child. His father had died three months before his birth, and when Newton was three, his mother remarried and left him in the care of his maternal grandmother. Newton reportedly disliked his stepfather and resented his mother for remarrying, as evidenced by a note in which he expressed a desire to burn them and their house. Newton began his education at local village schools and later attended The King's School in Grantham, where he excelled academically. He lodged with an apothecary named William Clarke and became engaged to Clarke's stepdaughter, Anne Storer, before leaving for the University of Cambridge at age 19. However, as Newton became absorbed in his studies, the romance faded, and Storer married someone else. Newton never married and is rumored to have remained celibate throughout his life. At Cambridge, Newton entered Trinity College as a sizar, a student who received financial assistance in exchange for performing menial tasks. The curriculum at the time was based on Aristotelian teachings, but Newton preferred the works of modern philosophers like Descartes and astronomers such as Copernicus, Galileo, and Kepler. In 1665, he discovered the generalized binomial theorem and began developing the mathematical framework that would later become calculus. After earning his degree in 1665, the university closed due to the Great Plague, and Newton returned home to Woolsthorpe. During this period, he developed his theories on calculus, optics, and gravitation. In mathematics, most historians agree that Newton and Leibniz independently developed calculus, each using their own notation. Newton's inner circle claimed he had devised his methods years before Leibniz, but he delayed publication until 1693 and did not provide a full account until 1704. Meanwhile, Leibniz published his methods in 1684, and his notation became widely adopted. This led to a bitter dispute between the two men, with accusations of plagiarism and a controversy that lasted until Leibniz's death in 1716. Newton is credited with the generalized binomial theorem, Newton's identities, and Newton's method for approximating roots. He classified cubic plane curves, contributed to the theory of finite differences, and was the first to use fractional indices and coordinate geometry to solve Diophantine equations. He also approximated partial sums of the harmonic series using logarithms and confidently employed power series. Newton was elected Lucasian Professor of Mathematics in 1669, a position that exempted him from the requirement to be ordained as an Anglican priest, thus avoiding a conflict between his religious views and church orthodoxy. From 1670 to 1672, Newton lectured on optics, investigating the refraction of light and demonstrating that a prism could decompose white light into a spectrum of colors. He showed that colored light does not change its properties when reflected, scattered, or transmitted, concluding that color results from objects interacting with pre-existing colored light. This became known as Newton's theory of color. He invented the reflecting telescope to address the dispersion of light in refracting telescopes, producing a superior instrument. In 1671, the Royal Society requested a demonstration of his telescope, encouraging him to publish his notes on color, which he later expanded into his book Opticks. Newton's work in optics led him to propose that light is composed of particles or corpuscles, which are refracted by accelerating toward denser media. However, he also associated these particles with waves to explain diffraction. Later physicists favored a wave-based explanation of light, and modern quantum mechanics incorporates the concept of wave-particle duality, which differs significantly from Newton's understanding. Newton's interest in alchemy and the occult influenced his scientific work. He replaced the concept of the ether with occult forces based on Hermetic ideas of attraction and repulsion between particles. John Maynard Keynes described Newton as the last of the magicians, emphasizing the connection between his alchemical pursuits and his scientific contributions. Newton's reliance on the idea of action at a distance across a vacuum was crucial to his development of the theory of gravity. In 1704, Newton published Opticks, expounding his corpuscular theory of light. He also constructed a primitive electrostatic generator using a glass globe. His work on gravitation and planetary motion, informed by Kepler's laws, culminated in the publication of Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica in 1687. This work introduced the three universal laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, which explained the motion of planets and other celestial bodies. Newton's postulation of an invisible force acting over vast distances drew criticism for introducing occult agencies into science. Newton's later years were marked by his role as Warden and then Master of the Royal Mint, where he oversaw the Great Recoinage of England. He took his duties seriously, reforming the currency and prosecuting counterfeiters. Newton's efforts against counterfeiters included disguising himself to gather evidence and conducting numerous cross-examinations. His most notable success was the conviction of William Chaloner, a notorious counterfeiter. Newton was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705, not for his scientific achievements but for his work at the Mint. He served as President of the Royal Society from 1703 and was an associate of the French Académie des Sciences. Newton died on March 31, 1727, and was buried in Westminster Abbey. His body was later found to contain high levels of mercury, likely due to his alchemical experiments, which may explain his eccentricity in later life. Newton's religious views were unorthodox, and he wrote extensively on theology. He rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and was likely a Socinian sympathizer or an Arian. He believed in a rationally ordered universe governed by a divine creator but warned against viewing the universe as a mere machine. Newton's theological writings, including his attempts to extract scientific information from the Bible, reflect his deep engagement with religious thought. Newton's influence extended beyond science to the Enlightenment, where his conception of a universe governed by natural laws inspired rationalist philosophers and political theorists. His work laid the foundation for the Enlightenment's emphasis on reason and the pursuit of knowledge.
